how: The room recruited members to draw the mascot and renewed calls when its work was being taken over.
Members answered the drawing call with bare commitments to join.
The starter explicitly attributed difficulty keeping the sprite whole to rival scripts and too few participants.
The member proposing the image supplied its location and received a direct commitment to join.
The proposed image represented the fandom through a character explicitly described as its half-mascot.
Members announced resumed work and reported missing or overwritten parts of the developing image.
Coordinates, reference images, and an answered colour question made the shared drawing actionable.
The room distributed browser-console script instructions and later explicitly reported working with scripts.
Participants watched disappearing features, called for help, and sought to keep the contested sprite whole.
Defending emerging features overlapped with unfinished construction rather than waiting for a completed mark.
A participant tentatively identified an encroaching logo and suggested contacting the implicated community.
Participants proposed negotiation, shared space, limits on expansion, and rebuilding terms with neighbours.
A warning about overlap received an explicit promise not to cover the neighbouring flag.
A neighbour's warning can elicit a restraint promise before any settled border is demonstrated.
Incoming proposals offered shared space or rebuilding help, and one reported offer received explicit acceptance.
Distinguish proposed help and accepted terms from evidence that the promised placements were delivered.
Reported openness to an alliance and acceptance of rebuilding terms precede any verified joint defence.
Alliance discussion is visible, but the cited turns do not document an operating coalition or completed joint defence.
The starter sought a less contested location after loss and then announced work resuming at new coordinates.
A participant reported talking to another community and brought its willingness to ally back into the thread.
Members praised everyone's effort and the honour of working together despite the missed goal.
Members can celebrate shared participation and a surviving fragment while explicitly acknowledging that the full goal failed.
Members marked Game Over, shared a final snapshot, and remembered the remnant of the first drawing.
An incoming proposal called for jointly displacing rival builders, without demonstrating that a raid occurred.
Participants cursed named rivals while helping and after the canvas closed.
Members recognised the Strega rumor as an April Fools joke and mocked the suggestion that it fooled anyone.
Treat prank recognition as reception unless evidence identifies the room as the prank's producer or connects it to the canvas call.
The room carried fandom lore into its mascot explanation and its Mighty Action rally.
A member's dual fandom does not establish a pre-canvas quarrel between the communities.
Participants identify contested pixels and rival scripts without citing an inherited rivalry as the reason for an attack.
One room cannot test cross-room prevalence, and visible instructions do not determine whether formal authority existed elsewhere.
Shared-space and relocation proposals do not show a host exercising rule over guests.
The coded moderator instructions organise placement without documenting a posting boundary or rule containing canvas talk.
The reported offer and assent do not disclose a dispute about who may bind the room.
Recording and appreciating a damaged remnant do not establish a dispute over cleanup or the version preserved.
Appreciating the surviving fragment does not document carrying the project into another canvas, organisation, or enduring relationship.
A greeting with a removed request supports contact alone unless surviving evidence specifies the help sought or offered.
A prank reveal prompted interest in its underlying character, a response distinct from exposing or extending the joke.
A member withheld a side because they belonged to both competing fandoms, qualifying the room-as-actor account without negotiating a border.
Explaining the mark to an outsider occurred during ongoing defence rather than only while decoding a finished canvas.
Relocation renewed coordination through a new location, sprite references, and an ensuing colour question.
The call, joins, and later work reports establish a sequence without measuring the call's effect on actual building.
Starter and recruitment can occur in the same proposal rather than requiring a separate later call.
The transition to upkeep protects partially built features and need not await completion of the whole mark.
Participants explicitly coupled takeover reports with proposals to negotiate or seek rebuilding partners.
A direct complaint and restraint promise do not establish the proposed mechanism of an already settled border governing subsequent compliance.
The last-stand post explicitly presents a newly found script as a response to rival takeovers.
Automation under attack may remain insufficient when rival scripts operate and participants still judge their numbers inadequate.
Explaining praise must allow valued participation and a surviving fragment as grounds even when the room explicitly failed its full goal.
Praise and a final snapshot coexist without a cited reply linking the praise to the decision to preserve the image.
The final record does not disclose a subsequent decision to reuse the work or retain a canvas-created organisation.
Judging hands too few does not select relocation when members can instead pursue an alliance and rebuilding at the contested spot.
The reference precedes a colour correction, without evidence that template publication settled a prior design debate.
A direct reply accepts the starter's drawing call with an unqualified commitment to join.
The observed bare acceptance supports written commitment but cannot determine silent placement or the form of unobserved refusals.
Strain and help offers are documented, but arrival of the promised external help remains unverified.
Negotiating and accepting a rebuilding offer is an intermediate outcome before any help delivery can be established.
Space-for-help terms demonstrate proposed reciprocity without verifying that border talk produced an executed exchange.
The record contains recruitment and adversarial proposals without showing that the call redirected placers from building to attack.
The flag complaint and restraint promise are not replies to the adversarial proposal, so the proposed refusal mechanism remains untested.
Negotiation and adversarial proposals coexist without a cited answer invoking a truce to reject an attack call.
The later curse does not explicitly answer or recall the earlier proposal to displace rivals.
Alliance openness under strain does not establish that a coalition formed and jointly defended the works.
Recruitment is visible without a coded flood of canvas posts producing a moderation boundary.
The offer and acceptance do not document a subsequent dispute over members being bound by the agreement.
